name: Thattukada Design Club
tagline: Honest design crits, served hot. Kochi's UI/UX and product design collective.
about:
Thattukada Design Club is named after the roadside food stalls that keep Kochi fed after dark: quick, hot, honest, and nobody cares what you're wearing. It began in 2021, when a handful of designers from agencies around MG Road started meeting at a thattukada near Kaloor to show each other work their bosses hadn't seen yet. The stall has gone. The habit stayed.

Today we're a few hundred UI and UX designers, product designers, illustrators, researchers and developers who care about how things look and work. Our signature is the Friday Crit: three people put real work on the screen and the room gives ten minutes each of specific, kind, unsparing feedback. Around it we run portfolio reviews, research workshops, a yearly show of interfaces made in Kerala, and the occasional walk to look at signboards.

We care about design that works for the people around us: the auto driver on a cracked Android phone, the grandmother who reads in Malayalam, the shop owner who has never heard the word 'onboarding'. If that's your kind of problem, pull up a stool.

events.name: Signboard Safari: A Type Walk Through Mattancherry
events.about:
A slow Sunday-morning walk through Mattancherry and Fort Kochi, looking at letters: hand-painted shop signs, enamel boards, Malayalam stencilled on spice-warehouse doors, Gujarati on old trading houses, and tea-shop menus with the same prices painted over for decades. Aysha leads with a sketchbook and stops every few hundred metres to explain why a letter is shaped the way it is.

Halfway through, we visit a sign painter who has worked in Mattancherry since 1989. We end at Nilavelicham Studio with appam and stew, and a short session where everyone redraws one sign they saw as a digital wordmark.
events.guidelines: Meet at 6:50 at the start of Bazaar Road; we leave at 7:00 sharp to beat the heat. The walk is about three kilometres on uneven pavements, so wear comfortable footwear. Ask before photographing people, and please don't touch or lean on old boards; some are held up by habit.

speakers.designation: Illustrator and letterer, Thattukada Design Club
speakers.bio: Has photographed more than two thousand Kerala shop signs and is writing a small book about the painters behind them.

speakers.name: Pradeep Chandrasekharan
speakers.bio: Has painted shop boards in Mattancherry since 1989 and still mixes his own enamel colours.

comments: I've walked Bazaar Road a hundred times and never looked up. It changed how I see the city.
Watching Pradeep chettan mix enamel by hand was the highlight of my month.
A little early for those of us coming from Aluva, but worth every minute.

events.name: Designing for the Cracked Screen

venue.name: Nilavelicham Studio
venue.address: 1st floor, Princess Street, Fort Kochi, Kochi 682001

events.about:
Most people using the apps we design aren't holding a new flagship. They're on a four-year-old phone with a cracked corner, brightness turned down to save battery, the font size set to large, and a network that drops in the lift. This workshop puts you in their shoes: we hand out a box of old phones with real cracks and ask you to finish five everyday tasks in apps you know.

After a morning of frustration, Arathi takes you through practical fixes: touch targets, contrast, Malayalam text that doesn't clip, loading states, and screens that still make sense at double the font size. In the afternoon, teams redesign one painful flow and test it on the same phones.
events.guidelines: Bring a laptop with your usual design tool. We provide the test phones; please return each one in the case it came in. Lunch, tea and snacks are covered by the fee. Certificates go to everyone who presents a redesign in the final session.

speakers.name: Arathi Vinod
speakers.bio: Tests every interface with a screen reader and a phone set to its largest font, and files the bugs nobody else finds.

speakers.name: Sajan Mukundan
speakers.bio: Designs a loan app used by self-help groups in Palakkad and Thrissur, and once watched a user tap a disabled button nineteen times.

agenda.title: The box of broken phones: five tasks
What we saw, and why it happens
Fixes that work: targets, contrast, script and scale
Team redesign of one painful flow
Test it on the same phones

questions.label: Which design tool will you bring?

comments: Paying a bill on a cracked phone at 30% brightness was humbling. No more grey-on-grey buttons from me.
The section on Malayalam text clipping was gold. Nobody talks about it.
The afternoon felt short for a full redesign plus testing.
Sajan's nineteen-taps story is now a sticky note on my monitor.
Great lunch, great room, great people.

events.name: The Kerala Interface Show 2026
events.about:
Our yearly show of interfaces made in Kerala, printed big and pinned to the walls of an old godown in Calvetty. Twenty-six projects this year: a fish auction app used at Munambam harbour, a ticketing kiosk for a temple festival, the ordering system of a Kozhikode biryani chain, an attendance app for teachers who would rather not use apps, and many more. Every wall shows the before, the after and the messy middle.

Designers stood by their work all evening to walk anyone through it. At seven, three of them gave short talks on the one decision they'd most like to undo. People's Choice went to the school attendance app, by a margin of eleven votes.
events.guidelines: Free and open to all. The godown is up one flight of stairs, with a ramp at the side entrance. Photography is welcome, but credit the designers when you post. People's Choice voting closes at 8:30.

speakers.name: Nimisha Paul
speakers.bio: Curates the show every year and personally pins up every print, usually with a crooked one she refuses to fix.

speakers.name: Hari Govindan
speakers.bio: Spent a year in government school staff rooms in Kollam watching teachers take attendance before designing anything.

speakers.name: Faseela Kunhammed
speakers.bio: Learned the hand signals of the Munambam auction floor before she drew a single screen.

questions.label: Are you showing work at the show?

comments: Seeing the before and after side by side, at that size, is something no online case study gives you.
The fish auction app blew my mind. Hand signals as an input method!
Too crowded around seven. Maybe split the talks into two slots?
Lovely to see so much work from outside Kochi this year.

events.name: Friday Crit #87: Bring Your Messy Work

venue.name: Nilavelicham Studio
venue.address: 1st floor, Princess Street, Fort Kochi, Kochi 682001

events.about:
Friday Crit is the oldest thing we do. Three people put real, unfinished work on the screen and get ten minutes each of specific, kind, unsparing feedback from the room. No polished case studies and no portfolio pieces. The messier the better: half-done flows, research you're unsure of, a logo you've stared at for too long.

This week's slots are open to anyone, first-timers included. If you'd rather just listen, come anyway. Most people do that for a few weeks before they present.
events.guidelines: Want to present? Answer the slot question in the form and we'll confirm by Wednesday. Keep it to one problem and ten minutes. Feedback follows our rules: be specific, critique the work and not the person, and say one thing that works before one that doesn't.

speakers.name: Nimisha Paul
speakers.bio: Has hosted eighty-six Friday Crits and still writes each piece of feedback on an index card for the presenter to keep.

speakers.name: Rahul Kesavadas
speakers.bio: Brings the research questions to every crit, usually starting with 'who did you watch use this?'

events.name: Research in the Wild: Two Days at Ernakulam Market

venue.name: Nilavelicham Studio
venue.address: 1st floor, Princess Street, Fort Kochi, Kochi 682001

events.about:
A two-day research intensive for designers who have run plenty of surveys and very few real conversations. On Saturday morning, Rahul teaches the basics of contextual inquiry in the studio; then the group heads to Ernakulam Market in pairs to watch how vendors take orders, keep track of credit and deal with digital payments. On Sunday we turn the notes into findings and argue about what they mean.

There are only twenty seats, because each pair needs a mentor close by. The fee covers two lunches, travel between the studio and the market, a printed field kit, and a stipend paid to every vendor who gives us their time.
events.guidelines: Wear light clothes and expect heat. Speak whichever language the vendor speaks; pairs are arranged so at least one person speaks Malayalam. Never record audio or take photos without asking, and never during a sale. Mentors hand out the vendor stipends, not participants.

speakers.name: Rahul Kesavadas
speakers.bio: Runs research for a Kochi health start-up and has spent more hours in Kerala markets than in meeting rooms.

speakers.name: Dr. Mini Abraham
speakers.bio: Has studied Kerala's wholesale markets for fifteen years and teaches designers how to listen without leading.
